paragraphs: Ibec is a group for Irish employers. It asked more than 300 companies about work and pensions. Ibec shared the results at a meeting in Dublin.

A new Government pension plan started this year. Now more companies have their own pension plans too. Almost half of them say all workers must join. Fewer companies now make new workers wait before they can join.
Companies also want people in the office more. More of them now ask for three days a week.
Most companies think AI will not change jobs much soon. Their biggest worry is new EU rules about pay. These rules come in 2027. Only one in five companies feels ready.
More Irish companies are offering pensions to their workers, and many are making them compulsory, according to a new survey by the employers' group Ibec.

Ibec asked more than 300 employers about trends at work. It found a 12% increase in companies with a workplace pension scheme since the Government started its auto-enrolment scheme. Almost half of companies (48%) now say all workers must join, and 81% say their scheme is open to everyone.
The survey also found that more companies want staff in the office. The number asking for three days a week rose from 31% to 35%. Companies said this helps productivity and attracts good workers.
Almost 60% of employers do not expect artificial intelligence to change jobs much in the next few years. However, 36% have not studied its effects yet.
The biggest worry for employers is new EU rules on pay transparency, which will come into Irish law in 2027. Only one in five companies feels well prepared.
The Government's new auto-enrolment scheme is reshaping workplace pensions, with more employers running their own schemes and many making them mandatory, according to a survey by business group Ibec.

Ibec's Trends report, based on responses from more than 300 employers, found a 12% rise in organisations offering an occupational pension and a 19% rise in voluntary schemes becoming compulsory. The share of firms requiring staff to complete a minimum period of service before joining halved, from 55% to 28%.

The survey also points to a stronger push for office attendance. The proportion of employers requiring three days a week on site rose from 31% to 35%, with productivity and attracting talent cited as the main reasons.
On artificial intelligence, almost 60% of firms expect no significant impact on headcount in the short to medium term, although 36% have yet to assess it.
Employers' biggest concern for the year ahead is pay transparency, as EU rules take effect in Ireland during 2027. Only a fifth say they are well prepared, while 10% have done nothing at all.

The State's auto-enrolment scheme is transforming the pensions landscape, prompting more employers to establish their own schemes and, in many cases, to make membership compulsory, a survey by employers' body Ibec has found.

Drawing on more than 300 employers, Ibec's Trends report records a 12% upswing in organisations running occupational pensions and a 19% increase in voluntary schemes being made mandatory. Meanwhile, the proportion imposing a minimum service period before staff can enrol has halved, from 55% to 28%.

The findings also reveal a renewed drive to bring staff back to their desks: the share of firms stipulating three office days a week climbed from 31% to 35%, with productivity and talent attraction the principal motivations.
Artificial intelligence, by contrast, is not expected to upend workforces imminently; nearly 60% of firms foresee little effect on headcount, though 36% have yet to model its implications.

Pay transparency looms largest on employers' agenda, with EU-mandated measures set to come into force in 2027. Tellingly, a mere fifth consider themselves well prepared, while 10% have done no groundwork whatsoever.

According to a survey conducted by the employers' organisation Ibec, the Government's auto-enrolment scheme is substantially altering the pensions landscape, as an increasing number of employers establish occupational schemes and render participation mandatory.

Ibec's Trends report, which draws upon responses from more than 300 employers, identified a 12% increase in organisations operating occupational pensions and a 19% increase in voluntary schemes becoming compulsory. Furthermore, the proportion of firms imposing a minimum period of service prior to enrolment declined from 55% to 28%.

The data also indicate a greater emphasis on office attendance: the proportion of employers requiring three days per week on site rose from 31% to 35%, with productivity and talent acquisition cited as the primary justifications.

Regarding artificial intelligence, almost 60% of firms anticipate no significant impact on staffing levels in the short to medium term; nevertheless, 36% have not yet evaluated its potential consequences.

Pay transparency constitutes employers' principal concern, given that EU measures are due to be implemented in Ireland in 2027. Only one fifth of respondents regard themselves as adequately prepared, whereas 10% have undertaken no preparation.
